title: Investors' ideology and corporate symbolic and substantive climate actions
authors: Chang Liu; Wei Shi
affiliations: CUHK Business School Chinese University of Hong Kong Hong Kong China; Miami Business School University of Miami Coral Gables Florida USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Prior research suggests that institutional investors' liberalism is associated with firms' engagement in environmental sustainability, yet whether this association manifests in symbolic or substantive actions remains unclear. Taking a question‐driven approach, our analyses of Russell 3000 firms (2010–2020) reveal that investor liberalism, measured as the proportion of donations made to the Democratic Party, is positively associated with symbolic climate actions only from 2016 onward (a period when political polarization intensified), reversing a negative association during 2010–2015. Its positive association with substantive actions from 2016 onward, however, appears only among consistent Democratic donors (stronger liberal values), among dedicated investors, or in firms without CEO duality (greater investor influence). These findings indicate that liberal investor ownership may encourage, rather than deter, firms' environmental decoupling. Managerial Summary Liberal institutional investors tend to favor greater corporate environmental sustainability efforts, but are they associated with firms' symbolic or substantive climate actions? Our findings based on U.S. firms reveal that across the full 2010–2020 period, firms with more liberal investors, as indicated by their Democratic‐leaning political donations, do not exhibit more symbolic or substantive climate actions. From 2016 onward, as political polarization intensified, firms with more liberal investors exhibited more symbolic climate actions but not substantive ones. During this period, only investors with stronger liberal commitment (i.e., consistent Democratic donors) are associated with more substantive actions. Democratic‐donating investors are also associated with more substantive actions when they are dedicated investors or when firm CEOs do not chair their boards.

title: Action-oriented Narratives. How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
authors: Claudio Biscaro; Arvind Malhotra; Ann Majchrzak
affiliations: Johannes Kepler Universität Linz, Institute of Leadership and Change Management, Linz, Austria; UNC at Chapel Hill, Kenan-Flagler Business School, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States; University of Southern California, Information Systems, Los Angeles, California, United States
abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

title: Semibandit Learning for Monotone Stochastic Optimization
authors: Rohan Ghuge; Zhengjia Zhuo; Arpit Agarwal; Viswanath Nagarajan
affiliations: Department of Information, Risk, and Operations Management, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan–Ann Arbor, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400076, India
abstract: Learning When Demand Is Unknown Airlines launching new routes cannot wait for years of historical data before deciding how many seats to offer at each fare or what prices to charge. They must learn when operating, often from incomplete feedback: selling 30 economy plus seats does not reveal whether demand was 30, 40, or more. In the accepted Operations Research paper “Semibandit Learning for Monotone Stochastic Optimization,” Rohan Ghuge, Zhengjia Zhuo, Arpit Agarwal, and Viswanath Nagarajan develop a general framework for such decisions. They identify a basic property, monotonicity, that allows an optimization method built for known demand distributions to become a learning algorithm for unknown distributions. The framework applies to airline and hotel revenue management, sequential posted pricing, and optimal-stopping problems. Even with partial, censored, or yes-or-no feedback, its cumulative performance gap grows essentially at the square root rate, best possible up to logarithmic factors. Firms can, therefore, improve decisions as data arrive without pausing operations for a separate data-gathering phase.

title: Disagreement and Bond PEAD
authors: Yoshio Nozawa; Yancheng Qiu; Yan Xiong
affiliations: University of Toronto, UTSC Management, Toronto, Ontario M1C 1A4, Canada; The University of Sydney Business School, Sydney, New South Wales 2006, Australia; Faculty of Business and Economics, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: This paper documents post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in corporate bond prices using transaction data. We find a counterintuitive relationship between the drift and trading volume: PEAD is more pronounced for more heavily traded bonds than for less frequently traded bonds. Across markets, PEAD is observed for credit default swaps but not for stocks. We explain these findings using a unified model that incorporates both debt and equity trading, where investors possess private information about the underlying firm’s cash flows and may hold differing opinions. Our empirical evidence supports the model’s prediction that payoff structures and investor disagreement account for the distinct price dynamics across asset classes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge research support from the Center for Investing at HKUST. Y. title: Conditional and Lenient Drug Approvals
authors: Chenxi Xu; Giuseppe Lopomo; David Ridley; Peng Sun
affiliations: Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr. School of Business, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907; Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina 27708
abstract: Firms are often allowed to sell new drugs based on preliminary efficacy evidence, with final approval contingent on confirmatory testing. We characterize optimal approval policies for a government agency that maximizes consumer welfare while considering the firm’s incentives. We assume that firms have private information about testing costs and the government’s payoff depends on the drug’s expected efficacy. The optimal policy may include partial conditional approval for drugs with low expected efficacy, and leniency in granting final approval below conventional standards. Our calibration suggests these tools can generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual social value. This paper was accepted by Martin Bichler, market design, platform, and demand analytics. title: Alert for Alerts: How Investment Price Tracking Alerts Affect Retail Investors1
authors: Yanzhen Chen; Che-Wei Liu; Ming-Hui Wen
affiliations: Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management, School of Business and Management The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China; Department of Information Systems, W. P. Carey School of Business Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, U.S.A.; Department of Commercial Design and Management, School of Innovative Design and Management National Taipei University of Business, Taipei, Taiwan
abstract: The burgeoning innovations in financial technology (fintech) are bringing powerful investment tools from Wall Street to Main Street. Among these tools, digital engagement practices (DEPs), such as price tracking alerts, have seen widespread adoption across online investment platforms. While the fintech industry positions these alerts as neutral, informational tools that enhance investor autonomy, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has raised concerns that such features may exploit behavioral biases and unintentionally harm retail investors. Motivated by this regulatory challenge, we introduce a regulation-centric framework (“what – why – who – how”) that explicitly links empirical analysis to the policy questions confronting regulators. This framework structures our analysis around four sequential questions: What is the effect of alerts on investor outcomes? Why do these effects arise—specifically, through which behavioral mechanisms? Who is most affected, based on investor characteristics and context? How should regulation respond in a targeted and enforceable manner? Using detailed account-level data from a major digital mutual fund platform, we found that alerts tend to reduce investor performance by increasing trading frequency and observed no evidence of increased risk-taking. With tracking alerts, investors are more likely to sell when prices rise with no corresponding change in selling when prices fall, a pattern consistent with the disposition effect. These effects were most pronounced among inexperienced and financially less literate investors, particularly when tracking volatile or unfamiliar assets. Our findings support a regulator-led model in which digital brokers are required to monitor, report, and refine DEPs under auditable, behaviorally informed standards. We offer evidence-based policy recommendations that balance investor protection with the continued advancement of fintech innovation.

title: Digital Resilience as a Process of Relational Resourcing1
authors: Angelos Kostis; Jonny Holmström; Stefan Haefliger
affiliations: Umeå School of Business, Economics and Statistics, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden; Management Science and Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, U.S.A.; Swedish Center for Digital Innovation, Department of Informatics, Umeå University Umeå, Sweden; House of Innovation, Stockholm School of Economics, Stockholm, SWEDEN, and Bayes Business School, City St. George’s University of London, London, UK
abstract: Digital resilience has become increasingly crucial for organizations and professionals in times of major exogenous shocks and escalating crises. Complementing capability-oriented accounts of digital resilience, we examined how resources are created through evolving relations, offering a process view of digital resilience. Through a longitudinal, qualitative study of Greek primary school teachers, we explored how digital resilience emerges through evolving relations despite limited organizational support. Drawing on a resourcing lens, our study establishes that digital resilience emerges and is sustained when professionals, motivated by value-laden beliefs that make them assume responsibility for turning potential resources into resources-in-use to respond to a shock, engage in a process we call relational resourcing. Our model of relational resourcing shows how resourcing convictions are enacted through processes including appropriating personal digital technologies, enlarging relational functionalities, and routinizing new enactments of resourcing convictions. Our findings expand resourcing theory by showing how resourcing activities entail new ways of relating from which resource value derives. Furthermore, the findings add to the relational view of technology by theorizing how and why entities or professionals learn to relate.

title: Innovation Orientation in New Product A Unified Framework of Backward-Looking and Forward-Looking Perspectives
authors: Yueyue Zhang; Xia Zhao; Ling Xue; Cheng Zhang
affiliations: University of Nottingham Ningbo China Ningbo, PR China; Terry College of Business, University of Georgia Athens, GA U.S.A.; School of Management, Fudan University Shanghai, PR China
abstract: This study develops an integrated framework to reconcile different theoretical lenses on how firms respond to expected competitive threats with different innovation orientations in new product development. The framework unifies both the forward-looking and backward-looking perspectives of organizational decision-making. We theorize how a firm’s past performance feedback (a key backward-looking factor) shapes the relationship between expected competitive threats (a key forward-looking factor) and product innovation orientation by influencing the firm’s sense of controllability, and how this effect is influenced by the firm’s information technology (IT) investment and alliance network structure. Based on an empirical analysis of 1,571 public US firms, we find that past performance feedback has a positive moderating effect on the relationship between expected competitive threats and product exploration orientation. Specifically, when the firm has unfavorable past performance feedback, the relationship between expected competitive threats and product exploration orientation is significantly negative, as predicted by the threat-rigidity theory. However, when the firm has favorable past performance feedback, this relationship becomes positive, as predicted by the Behavioral Theory of the Firm. We theorize and empirically verify that the sense of controllability derived from past performance feedback explains firms’ divergence in the framing of competitive threats and subsequent production innovation decision-making. Moreover, we find that the positive moderating effect of past performance feedback is alleviated when the firm has higher information processing capabilities (proxied by higher IT investment) or more external information access (proxied by a higher level of structural holes in its alliance network). Further examination suggests that greater information processing capabilities and information access allow firms to maintain a sense of control when expecting heightened competitive threats. These findings highlight the importance of information within the unified theoretical framework of both the backward-looking and forward-looking perspectives for product innovation.

title: “Phygital” Experiences: Optimization, Tailoring, and Pricing Contract Strategies on Online Platforms1
authors: Hongseok Jang; Kyung Sung Jung; Young Kwark
affiliations: Freeman School of Business, Tulane University New Orleans, LA, U.S.A.; Department of Information Systems, Korea University Business School (KUBS), Korea University Seoul, Republic of Korea; Department of Business Information and Analytics, Daniels College of Business, University of Denver, Denver, CO, U.S.A.
abstract: Technology-driven tools, such as augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), bring products to life in a virtual space for online consumers and are poised to become the new standard. With more effective tools, consumers are more likely to find the products that best meet their needs. While these tools enhance online purchasing decisions, consumers vary in their ability to use them effectively. As e-shopping continues to grow, firms must carefully consider whether and how to offer these tools. In this paper, we analytically study the firm’s (1) tool provision, (2) the optimization of a tool that brings a physical experience to e-shopping, and how they differ depending on (3) the heterogeneity of consumer expertise in using the tool. We also consider (4) pricing decisions, different channel contracts, and (5) the alignment of profits with the platform through which the firm sells its products with respect to tool optimization and tailoring incentives. We find that a tool need not always be perfect; experienced users can be given an imperfect tool. Although optimal effectiveness can be higher when a tool is tailored to inexperienced users, sellers do not pursue this strategy, as it primarily benefits the platform. While the platform does not always have the same incentives as the seller in dimensions such as tool provision, pricing contracts, and tailoring preferences, we find that this misalignment in tailoring preferences can be mitigated for certain product categories. Additionally, our results show that optimal tool effectiveness is always higher under a sell-on contract, making it a potential win-win solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that tool provision can shift the platform’s preference from a sell-to to a sell-on contract, which generally benefits the seller. Altogether, we show that tool provision should be considered jointly with tailoring to different consumer experience levels. Our results remain robust when accounting for a mix of inexperienced and experienced consumers, product returns, risk-averse consumers, and cost barriers.

title: Collective Attention Configurations in Open-Source Software Development: Interlacing for High Performance1
authors: Yanran Liu; Arun Rai
affiliations: Department of Operations, Business Analytics, and Information Systems, Lindner College of Business, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, U.S.A.; Center for Digital Innovation and Computer Information Systems Department, Robinson College of Business, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, U.S.A.
abstract: Coordinating open-source software (OSS) development requires both the division and integration of developers’ attention. How to combine these contradictory logics effectively, however, remains unclear. Adopting a configurational lens, we distinguish between developers’ primary attention, or their top-priority focus, and secondary attention, or their spare capacity. Along these two lines, division and integration take on different forms. Recombining these forms yields two new coordination logics: interlacing, which combines primary division with secondary integration, and interlocking, which combines primary integration with secondary division. Applying the same or different logics across OSS’s two key work types—discursive and technical—produces a broader set of coordination configurations. Analyzing 4,291 release cycles from 1,004 GitHub machine-learning projects, we find that isomorphic interlacing—applying interlacing in both work types—delivers the strongest performance of development speed, novelty, and quality. Configurations pairing interlacing with division or integration also perform well under particular contingencies of task interdependence, project ownership, and release-cycle length. By contrast, configurations involving interlocking consistently underperform. Our study advances OSS coordination theory by identifying a high-performing configuration that systematically combines division and integration and clarifying when alternative configurations can substitute for it.

title: A Generalist Activity Paradox: Individual Performance and Collective Production Efficiency on Open Innovation Platforms
authors: Lusi Yang; Zhiyi Wang; Steven L. Johnson
affiliations: J. Mark Robinson College of Business, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA U.S.A.; Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO U.S.A.; McIntire School of Commerce, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA U.S.A.
abstract: This study examines the relationship between generalist activity and multilevel performance on open innovation platforms for new product development. In such settings, task decomposition allows contributors to engage flexibly across multiple task types, giving rise to generalist activity, defined as the distribution of engagement across a wide variety of task types. Drawing on the generalist literature and the theory of collective production, we theorize how generalist activity relates to both individual and collective performance of crowds. Our multilevel framework and empirical findings indicate that generalist activity is positively associated with individual performance. However, due to the emergent nature of collaboration, a higher level of generalist activity within a crowd is associated with lower collective production efficiency, revealing a multilevel tension. This tension is attenuated as the crowd size increases. Mechanism analysis further shows that valuable contributions are more likely to emerge when contributors with generalist activity build upon task-focused inputs from preceding contributors with low levels of generalist activity. Overall, this study provides theoretical implications for open innovation platform research, generalist literature, and the theory of collective production.

title: Reconceptualizing Patient Engagement with Mobile Healthcare Apps: A Computationally Intensive Theory Development for Patient Engagement Networks
authors: Inkyoung Hur; Chul Woo Yoo; Jahyun Goo; Weidong Xia
affiliations: Department of Information Technology and Operations Management, College of Business, Florida Atlantic University, Baca Raton, FL, USA; Department of Information Systems and Business Analytics, College of Business, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
abstract: Mobile healthcare apps are increasingly used to enhance patient engagement, yet research has rarely examined the underlying mechanisms that shape this engagement. Addressing this gap, the present study adopts a computationally intensive theory development approach to explore how mobile healthcare apps afford patient engagement. To this end, rather than focusing on isolated app affordances, we examine affordance networks – interconnected patterns of app usage by patients and clinicians – and their association with diverse engagement goals. Through empirical analysis and an abductive reasoning process, we reconceptualize patient engagement with mobile healthcare apps as Patient Engagement Networks (PENs): linked sets of collaborative digital actions between patients and/or clinicians, enacted by mobile healthcare apps, that support the pursuit of healthcare goals. We propose four distinct modes of PENs, such as emergent, time-deliberate, supportive, and self-service, each reflecting a unique configuration of engagement. These findings offer valuable theoretical and practical insights into the evolving nature of digital healthcare interactions.

title: Outcome Over Process: Advancing Both Fairness and Performance in Crowdfunding Through ML-Assisted Promotion
authors: Lauren Rhue; Jessica Clark
affiliations: Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland – College Park College Park, MD U.S.A.
abstract: Crowdfunding platforms can influence project success through their promotion policy, which determines which projects receive enhanced visibility. Promotion policies can directly influence inclusivity on the platform and potentially address well-documented disparities across creators. This study examines how alternative machine learning (ML) problem framings for promotion policy affect fairness and business performance. Using data from 118,780 Kickstarter projects, we compare three ML framings: a process framing that learns to reproduce historical employee promotion decisions, a success framing that predicts whether projects will meet their funding goals, and a backers framing that predicts whether projects will attract a large number of backers. We evaluate the resulting counterfactual promotion sets using multiple fairness and performance measures. In our context, the success framing produces promotion sets with more favorable fairness outcomes and business performance outcomes than the other framings, possibly because it applies more consistent promotion decisions across similar projects. These findings demonstrate that alternative ML problem framings can produce meaningfully different promotion policies, even when trained on the same underlying data. While the success framing prioritizes practical projects, the backers framing favors projects with higher funding goals. Importantly, carefully designing the ML problem framing for promotion policies can align fairness and performance objectives, countering concerns that inclusivity necessarily comes at the expense of performance. This research contributes to the information systems literature by demonstrating that ML problem framing is a consequential choice in platform governance. It offers practical guidance for digital platforms seeking to improve fairness and business performance through ML-assisted promotion policies.

title: Immersion in Online Interaction Rituals: The Paradoxical Role of Time-Synchronized Comments on Video Platforms
authors: Yijing Li; Kai H. Lim; Fei Liu; Yao Li
affiliations: Faculty of Business, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, SAR, China
abstract: Many video platforms promote time-synchronized comments (TSCs), comments overlaid on videos in sync with specific timestamps, to facilitate social interaction and enhance video engagement. Yet TSCs can both enrich viewing experiences and distract viewers, thereby reducing engagement. Because TSCs appear as continuous overlaid streams that offer viewers little control over pacing or selection, their structural features may shape interaction in opposing ways. Drawing on interaction ritual theory, we identify two such features, comment density and word density, and examine their effects on video engagement, together with the moderating roles of content characteristics of both TSCs and videos. We test our framework through a field study using panel data from a leading TSC-enabled platform and a psychophysiological experiment that captures viewers’ real-time attentional, emotional, and behavioral responses. The results show that higher comment density strengthens perceived assembly, mutual focus of attention, and emotional entrainment, thereby increasing engagement. By contrast, greater word density disrupts mutual focus and emotional entrainment, thereby reducing engagement. Emotional entrainment emerges as the central mechanism. We also find that these effects vary with TSC emotional polarization and video genre. In addition, we test a reduced visual overlay design that mitigates the negative effects of TSCs. By clarifying how, when, and why TSCs enhance or disrupt engagement, this study extends understanding of micro-level social interaction in mediated contexts and offers guidance for improving TSC-enabled video experiences.

title: From Monologue to Dialogue: Remaking Public Service Communication with Celebrity-as-a-Service
authors: Antino Kim; Lingyao (Ivy) Yuan; Mike Seymour; Alan R. Dennis
affiliations: Operations & Decision Technologies Department, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN U.S.A.; Department of Information Systems and Business Analytics, Debbie & Jerry Ivy College of Business, Iowa State University, Ames, IA U.S.A.; School of Strategy, Innovation and Technology, The University of Sydney Darlington, New South Wales 2006, Australia; Operations & Decision Technologies Department, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University Bloomington, IN U.S.A.
abstract: Public service communication aims to raise awareness and change behaviors on critical public issues, such as health, safety, and the environment. Public service communication typically takes one of two forms: a public service announcement (PSA), such as a TV or radio advertisement that broadcasts information (a monologue), or a public service interaction (PSI), such as a meeting with officials that both provides and collects information (a dialogue). Celebrity involvement has traditionally been limited to PSAs due to cost and scalability challenges, but advancements in AI now enable the use of digital humans as scalable, interactive “celebrity-as-a-service” solutions. These AI-controlled digital celebrities mimic real people, enabling one-on-one celebrity interactions at scale. In an online experiment, we compared a digital celebrity to a non-celebrity digital human delivering a skin cancer awareness message in both a PSA and a one-on-one PSI. Results showed that both perceived celebrity (celebrity vs. non-celebrity) and interactivity (PSI vs. PSA) increased trustworthiness and enjoyment. Trustworthiness, in turn, increased the intention to comply with the public service message, while both trustworthiness and enjoyment increased the likelihood of sharing the message. We conclude that AI-controlled digital celebrities open the door to incorporating celebrities into one-on-one PSIs to drive more effective, scalable, and cost-effective public service communication.

title: Quo Vadis (IT) Strategy? Rethinking Strategy Within Digital Logic
authors: Gabriele Piccoli; Kalle Lyytinen; Varun Grover
affiliations: Stephenson Department of Entrepreneurship & Information Systems, E. J. Ourso College of Business, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA; Department of Economics and Management, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy; Department of Design & Innovation, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH, USA; Stockholm School of Economics, House of Innovation, Stockholm, Sweden; Department of Information Systems, Walton College of Business, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract: A growing consensus holds that digital strategy is business strategy. Yet, scholarship on the digital-strategy nexus lacks a first-principled definition of digital strategy, one grounded in the unique ontology of digital objects and a framework to conceptualize it in a manner that captures the novel realities of today's pervasive digital operations and the organizing logic that governs them. This paper addresses the gap by offering a foundational reframing of firm-level strategy guided by the principles of digital logic – the economic regime of value creation and capture predicated on the primacy of digital objects and their runtime orchestration into digital service stacks. We draw on the core guidance view of strategy and define digital strategy as the smallest set of scope, value proposition, and functional choices that, subordinate to the primacy of digital objects, optimally guides all other firm decisions. Based on the definition, we advance a framework for digital strategy formulation and execution comprising three recursive, interdependent activities: digital visioning, digital service stack architecting, and leverage point recognition and manipulation. These activities guide the coherent configuration and deployment of digital service stacks, including their operational, virtual, and contextual embeddings. We use the illustrative case of a century-old, global heavy equipment manufacturer to demonstrate how the firm reframed its strategy under digital logic. The proposed theory advances scholarship on digital strategy by foregrounding the ontology of digital objects and establishes a metatheoretical foundation for future research on digital strategy.

title: Detecting and Correcting Estimation Bias Caused by Content Deletion in User-generated Content Studies
authors: Mengke Qiao; Qinglai He; Ke-Wei Huang
affiliations: Department of Information Systems, Statistics, & Management Science Culverhouse College of Business, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL U.S.A.; Department of Operations and Information Management Wisconsin School of Business, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI U.S.A.; Department of Information Systems and Analytics, School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore
abstract: User-generated content (UGC) platforms increasingly enable content deletion to manage the online environment and user-posted content, which contributes to missing data issues in empirical research involving UGC data. Such missingness may be correlated with the unobserved data, resulting in the most challenging missingness type–Missing Not at Random (MNAR), which can lead to biased estimates in empirical analyses. Despite its prevalence, limited scholarly attention has been given to the missing data challenges arising from content deletion, and researchers lack theoretical guidance for diagnosing and handling such missingness. In this study, we conduct an in-depth investigation of the reasons for content deletion across various UGC platforms and identify variables susceptible to the MNAR issue in empirical studies. We also develop a theoretical framework for diagnosing missingness mechanisms and selecting appropriate correction methods. Most importantly, we propose theoretical formulas to correct biased estimation in two MNAR scenarios for scale-level studies. Extensive simulations and sensitivity tests demonstrate that our proposed methods effectively reduce the estimation bias under scale-level MNAR compared to benchmark approaches. Collectively, our work advances the missing data literature and provides practical implications for empirical researchers.

title: Intelligent Approach to Discovering a New Functional Model Quantifying the Long-Tail Distribution of Online Markets
authors: Xian Yang; Zhijie Lin; Yuanfeng Cai
affiliations: School of Economics and Management, China University of Petroleum Beijing, China; School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University Beijing, China; Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College, City University of New York New York, U.S.A.
abstract: Actual sales data are valuable but often inaccessible. Thus, researchers and practitioners rely on sales–sales rank relationship models, such as the power-law distribution, to infer sales information. However, these models often poorly fit the sales distribution of online markets due to the long-tail phenomenon, creating a need for a more precise functional model. This paper proposes a novel model discovery framework, genetic programming with two-phase pruning (GPTP), which combines genetic programming with a newly developed two-phase pruning method to automatically learn a functional model relating sales to sales rank. Through analysis of sales data from both offline and online markets for 203,994 product items in 148 categories, we discover a new natural-power-law model that outperforms the traditional power-law model and provides a more accurate mathematical means of quantifying the long-tail distribution in online markets. The findings demonstrate that the proposed GPTP framework can intelligently learn the generalized knowledge underlying large business datasets and precisely determine the universal functional relationship model across multiple product categories in a white-box manner. The new model will enable researchers and practitioners to more accurately predict actual sales and explore various marketing issues.

title: Cross-Platform Links: Blessing or Curse?
authors: Jianchao Sheng; Jianqing Chen
affiliations: Faculty of Business for Science & Technology, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui, China; Jindal School of Management, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX, U.S.A.
abstract: In the digital-content industry, platforms compete to attract users and earn advertising revenue from content consumption. Conventional wisdom suggests that platforms should restrict cross-platform links to avoid user loss. However, practices of several platforms, such as TikTok—where content creators can include links in their profiles to competing platforms like YouTube—seem to contradict this notion, facilitating users’ exploration of preferred content elsewhere. In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model to examine two competing platforms’ strategies regarding cross-platform links. We find that the equilibrium strategies are driven by two opposing effects. On one hand, the cross-platform link causes users with high degrees of misfit to be redirected to the rival platform, resulting in a consumption-loss effect. On the other hand, the cross-platform link motivates the creator to enhance content quality, which not only attracts more users but also helps them find preferred content through the link. This quality-enhancement effect benefits the platform by increasing consumption from users who remain on the platform. The trade-off between these two opposing effects depends critically on the misfit between users and content, as well as the average advertising revenue generated from content consumption (i.e., the advertising rate). Our analysis shows that, in the presence of a regular creator, when the unit misfit cost is high, both platforms allow cross-platform links in equilibrium. When both the unit misfit cost and the advertising rate are low, both platforms ban the link in equilibrium. When the unit misfit cost is low and the advertising rate is high, both allowing and banning the link can be possible equilibrium outcomes. Furthermore, we show that the cross-platform link benefits both the creator and users, and both platforms opting to ban cross-platform links creates a prisoner’s dilemma even in terms of their revenues, warranting the attention of platform regulators.

title: How Generative AI Transforms Questioning Behavior on Q&A Platforms: Evidence from a Natural Experiment with Pilot Usage of ChatGPT
authors: Xinzhi Rao; Guohou Shan; Michael Rivera; Liangfei Qiu; Nan Wang
affiliations: Department of Information Systems and Operations Management, Warrington College of Business, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL U.S.A.; Department of Supply Chain and Information Management, D’Amore-McKim School of Business, Northeastern University, Boston, MA U.S.A.; Department of Decision and Technology Analytics, College of Business, Lehigh University Bethlehem, PA U.S.A.; Department of Leadership and Organization Management, School of Economics and Management, Beihang University, Beijing, China
abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI has enabled the automated generation of answers, introducing new dynamics in user behavior related to question-asking on digital platforms. However, the impact of users’ experience with generative AI for answer generation on their questioning behavior remains unclear. On the one hand, the availability of generative AI tools may lead users to rely on these tools for formulating questions, potentially resulting in fewer but higher-quality inquiries. On the other hand, using generative AI may motivate users to ask more questions to enhance their knowledge and build social reputation within the community. We investigate how the use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, to generate answers affects users’ questioning behavior on Stack Overflow, one of the largest Q&A platforms. Leveraging a natural experiment involving the introduction and subsequent ban of ChatGPT on the platform, we apply a difference-in-differences (DID) estimation approach to assess the effects of generative AI usage on the quantity and quality of user-generated questions. We measure these outcomes through metrics such as the number of questions posted per week, question length, novelty, and the number of received upvotes. Our findings reveal that the use of generative AI to generate answers is associated with an increase in the number of questions, which feature longer, more novel content and receive more upvotes. We examine two mechanisms: complexity shift, where ChatGPT handles routine queries while more advanced queries remain for the community, and skill enhancement, where users learn from ChatGPT to ask clearer questions. We also test two moderators: answer volume (proxy for user experience) and platform reputation score (proxy for user reputation). Results show weaker effects among experienced answerers but stronger effects among high reputation users. These insights highlight how generative AI shapes engagement and can guide platform strategies for AI integration.

title: Technology-Mediated Services in Health Care: Evaluating Telehealth Delivery Models for Underserved Populations
authors: Kyuyeon (Jenny) Rhee; Xiao Liu; Suparerk Lekwijit; Pei-Yu Chen
affiliations: Arizona State University, Information Systems, Tempe, Arizona, United States; Arizona State University W P Carey School of Business, Information Systems, Tempe, Arizona, United States
abstract: This study examines how telehealth delivery models are associated with access to care and protocol adherence in underserved populations. While prior research reports mixed evidence on telehealth’s effectiveness, we argue that these inconsistencies arise because telehealth is not a single intervention but is implemented through distinct service configurations that address different barriers. Drawing on the theoretical framework of digital economics, we conceptualize telehealth as a technology-mediated service that can alter key economic frictions, including search and verification, transportation, tracking, and setup costs. We focus on two widely adopted models—specialist-facilitated telehealth and remote telehealth—and theorize that each addresses different subsets of these frictions, leading to distinct effects on care access and protocol adherence across settings. Using panel data from U.S. Community Health Centers on mental health services, we document three findings. First, adoption of the specialist-facilitated model is associated with increased access to mental health care, particularly in areas with greater clinical need. Second, remote telehealth is not associated with increased access on average but is associated with higher adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. These effects are consistent with improvements in screening and documentation processes rather than increases in utilization. Third, the estimated effects of both models vary across local cost environments. The access effects of specialist-facilitated telehealth are larger in areas where search and verification frictions are greater. In contrast, the effects of remote telehealth are attenuated where patient-side setup costs are high but are larger where transportation barriers and documentation frictions are greater. These findings advance a model-specific perspective on telehealth’s effects, extend the digital economics framework to technology-mediated services, and provide evidence that the estimated effects of digital health interventions vary with how delivery models interact with underlying cost environments.

title: Does Private Equity Hurt or Improve Healthcare Value? New Evidence and Mechanisms
authors: Minghong Yuan; Wen Wen; Indranil Roy Bardhan
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Information Risk and Operations Management, Austin, Texas, United States; The University of Texas at Austin, McCombs School of Business, Austin, Texas, United States; The University of Texas at Austin, Information, Risk & Operations Management, Austin, Texas, United States
abstract: What is the impact of private equity (PE) ownership on healthcare value? Does PE ownership reduce healthcare value, and if so, can its effect be mitigated using health information technologies (IT)? Given the significant investments by PE firms in the healthcare sector in recent years, it is increasingly important for stakeholders, including policy makers, care providers, and patients, to understand their likely impact and whether PE ownership is aligned with their interests. Because PE firms seek to improve efficiency and generate short-term financial returns, the cost-cutting strategies used to achieve these goals may come at the expense of care quality, leading to competing hypotheses on the impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. We argue that IT-enabled health information sharing capabilities can help PE-owned hospitals to better manage this cost-quality tension and achieve higher healthcare value. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach and data from US hospitals from 2008 to 2020, we estimate changes in healthcare value following PE acquisition and ownership. Overall, we find that PE ownership of hospitals reduces healthcare value. This decline is partially driven by reduction in clinical staffing following PE ownership. We further find that pre-existing, hospital health information sharing capabilities mitigate the negative impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. Specifically, such capabilities can strengthen the effect of PE ownership on cost reduction and, at the same time, mitigate PE-induced, care quality deterioration. Our results highlight the critical role of common data standards needed to promote IT-enabled information sharing between healthcare providers, which, in turn, can align the incentives of PE firms with the goals of value-based care.

title: Symbolic governance and the spatial politics of disorder: Anti-social behaviour in Belfast’s ‘Holyland’
authors: Graham Ellison; Louise Rhodes
affiliations: School of Law, Queen’s University, Belfast, UK
abstract: This article examines how urban disorder is governed under conditions of contested legitimacy in a post-conflict city. Drawing on documentary analysis of institutional and policy materials from 2004 to 2025, it develops the concept of symbolic governance, defined as calibrated legitimacy management through which institutions regulate disorder while avoiding politically or reputationally risky intervention. Using Belfast’s Holyland district as an empirical site, the article traces how this logic operates across universities, policing, and local government. Revisiting social disorganisation theory, it argues that disorder is sustained not by weak social ties but by dense bonding networks within a demographically homogeneous enclave. Institutions respond through coordinated restraint and diffusion of responsibility, containing disorder within reputational thresholds while prioritising legitimacy over structural transformation.

title: Polycrisis and global production networks: a framework for understanding industry dynamics in times of accumulated uncertainty
authors: Lotte Thomsen; Shyamain Wickramasingha; Adrian Smith

abstract: Abstract Global production networks (GPNs) are currently impacted by multiple crises. Yet, crises have received little attention in GPN scholarship. This article shows how the entangled drivers of polycrisis affect the economic geographies of suppliers and their integration into GPNs. It develops an analytical framework for exploration of accumulated uncertainties in conjunctural moments of polycrisis. The management of unknown ‘uncertainties’ other than ‘risk’ for lead firms is a key element. Focusing on Bangladesh’s apparel industry, this article explores the industry’s responses and struggles, and provides insights into the wider processes of inclusion and exclusion in the global economy during polycrisis.

title: Balancing risk communication and accountability concerns in risk management: A study of major public project investments
authors: Sof Thrane; Ulrik Christiansen; Torben Juul Andersen; Giulio Zichella
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School , Solbjerg plads 3, 2000 Frederiksberg,; Copenhagen Business School & ISS, Solbjerg plads 3, 2000 Frederiksberg,; Copenhagen Business School , Porcelænshaven 24, 2000 Frederiksberg,
abstract: Abstract Effective administration of public organizations requires timely responses to emerging risks, yet communicating those risks up the hierarchy can expose operational managers to blame in politicized accountability environments. This study examines how public managers navigated that tension in an analysis of 130 risk reports filed over a seven-year period associated with two major procurement and maintenance projects in the Danish Defence. Using an abductive qualitative approach, we develop a dynamic model of risk management with four phases: (1) risk as an operational concern, (2) turning risk into an organizational problem, (3) assigning blame and accountability, and (4) initiating mitigation and response. We find that risk and accountability communication are interdependent processes rather than independent sequential processes. Operational managers attempt to raise awareness of emerging risks while simultaneously deflecting potential blame and catering to higher-level concerns about public scrutiny. This tension generates pressure to only report when it is absolutely necessary, while higher-level managers often postpone action to avoid political exposure. These practices contribute to delays, projects not meeting specifications, and significant budget overruns. The study advances a dynamic theory of public sector risk management and explains how hierarchical communication practices influence whether, when, and how emerging risks are addressed.

title: Solutions of two-stage stochastic minimax problems
authors: Hailin Sun; Xiaojun Chen
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a class of two-stage stochastic minimax problems where the first-stage objective function is nonconvex-concave while the second-stage objective function is strongly convex-concave. We establish properties of the second-stage minimax value function and solution functions, and characterize the existence and relationships among saddle points, minimax points, and KKT points. We apply the sample average approximation (SAA) to the class of two-stage stochastic minimax problems and prove the convergence of the KKT points as the sample size tends to infinity. An inexact parallel proximal gradient descent ascent algorithm is proposed to solve this class of problems with the SAA. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and validate the convergence properties of the SAA approach.

title: EXPRESS: Assortment Optimization Given Basket Shopping Behavior Using the Ising Model
authors: Andrey Vasilyev; Sebastian Maier; Ralf W. Seifert
abstract: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

title: EXPRESS: Improving Operational Performance through Boarding Time Slack: Evidence from the U.S. Airline Industry
authors: Chandrasekhar Manchiraju; Ashutosh Bhave; Milind G. Sohoni
abstract: Flight delays have a significant impact on airlines, passengers, and the U.S. economy. Airlines also use flight on-time performance (OTP) – a metric based on the proportion of delayed flights – to attract travelers by demonstrating service reliability. It is well established that adding buffers to flight time and ground time improves on-time arrivals. However, such buffers can impose significant costs. The flight and ground times comprise multiple activities, and prior research has primarily focused on studying the impact of aggregate buffers. In this paper, we study the impact of increasing the buffer of a critical ground time activity, namely boarding time, potentially without increasing the aggregate ground time buffer, on flight delays. To do so, we use the context of Delta Air Lines' recent policy changes wherein the airline increased the boarding time for domestic narrow-body flights by 5 minutes and started compensating flight attendants for pre-flight boarding. Using a Difference-in-Difference-in-Differences framework, we analyze and quantify the impact of these policies on Delta’s flight delays. Our findings indicate a significant reduction in departure delays following the policy changes, with increased boarding time playing a critical role in improving on-time departures. Our analysis finds no evidence that boarding compensation contributed to the improvement in on-time departures. We show that the increase in boarding time can improve the likelihood of on-time departures, potentially without requiring additional total ground time or incurring additional scheduling costs. We observe that the benefit is more pronounced for longer flights, busier routes, and later departures in the day. Airlines are often criticized for relying on costly, ad hoc schedule buffering to improve OTP. However, our results demonstrate that carefully planning buffer time for critical activities can significantly improve operational performance.

title: National Wage Contracts, Monopsony, and Welfare in a North-South Economy,
authors: Emanuele Ciani; Alberto Dalmazzo; Guido de Blasio
affiliations: Bank of Italy ,; University of Siena Deptment of Economics & Statistics, ,
abstract: Abstract In countries characterized by significant geographical disparities in productivity, nationwide labour contracts may cause local unemployment by preventing the adjustments that would occur in a competitive labour market. Here we argue, however, that when there are mobility frictions and monopsony power, nationwide contracts may still be preferable to local contracts. Using a spatial general equilibrium model calibrated on the Italian North-South divide, we suggest that nationwide wage contracts may still lead to narrower regional welfare gaps if monopsony power is sufficiently strong in low-productivity areas.

title: Growing Pains: Inefficient Resource Allocation in Emerging Economies
authors: Li Anpeng
affiliations: Liaoning University Shenyang People's Republic of China
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates how economic catch‐up shapes resource allocation in emerging economies. I develop a model that features firm‐specific technology adoption and costly adjustment of production factors. Rapid technological progress during catch‐up creates strong demand for reallocating resources from slow to fast adopters, amplifying the consequences of adjustment costs. The amplification fades as technological change gradually slows during convergence to a more advanced and efficient steady state. I evaluate the model using Chinese and German enterprise data and find that differences in development stage account for at least 40% of their labour allocative efficiency gap.

title: The Immigration Surplus Revisited
authors: Michael Amior; Alan Manning
affiliations: King’s College London; Hebrew University of Jerusalem; Centre for Economic Performance; London School of Economics
abstract: Abstract We extend the immigration surplus results of Borjas (1995). In a closed competitive constant-returns economy, we show that an influx of migrants (holding their skill mix fixed) must increase the total real income of natives, for any number of factor inputs, any pattern of substitutability or complementarity between them, and any number of intermediate or final goods – with larger gains if natives and migrants differ more in skill mix. If natives supply labour elastically across skill types, their welfare gains are diminished, even if they respond by moving to higher-paying jobs. We illustrate our results using a US calibration.

title: Networks of Dissent: Social Leaders and Protest in an Autocracy
authors: Johannes Buggle; Max Deter; Martin Lange
affiliations: University of Innsbruck; Berlin School of Economics, University of Potsdam , CEPA; ZEW Mannheim
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how network ties between local social leaders influenced the diffusion of mass protests in an autocracy. We focus on the Protestant Church and the Peaceful Revolution in East Germany. To quantify the role of leader networks in protest diffusion, we compile biographical records of over 1,600 Protestant pastors and construct network ties based on shared employment histories. Our findings reveal that network connections led to an increase in protest diffusion by 7.1 percentage points in a given week. Evidence from quasi-random connections, placebo networks, and an IV strategy supports a causal interpretation of these results.

title: TRUE AND PSEUDO-TRUE PARAMETERS
authors: Isaiah Andrews; Harvey Barnhard; Jacob Carlson
affiliations: MIT and NBER; Harvard University
abstract: Parameter estimates in misspecified models converge to pseudo-true parameter values, which minimize a population objective function. Pseudo-true values often differ from quantities of economic interest, raising questions of how, if at all, they are relevant for decision-making. To study this question, we consider Bayesian decision-makers facing a linear population minimum distance problem. Within a class of priors motivated by the minimum distance objective, we characterize prior sequences under which posteriors concentrate on the pseudo-true value. This convergence is fragile to small changes in priors, implying that pseudo-true values are relevant for decision-making only in special cases. Constructive results are nevertheless possible in this setting, and we derive simple confidence intervals that guarantee correct average coverage for the true parameter under every prior in the class we study, with no bound on the magnitude of misspecification.

title: PHILLIPS–SOLO ASYMPTOTICS FOR CONTINUOUS-TIME ARMA PROCESSES SAMPLED IN DISCRETE TIME
authors: Marcus J. Chambers
affiliations: University of Essex
abstract: Phillips and Solo (1992, Annals of Statistics 20, 971–2001) provided sets of conditions concerning the summability of coefficients and the properties of innovations in discrete-time linear processes such that normalized sums satisfy certain asymptotic properties, such as laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, and invariance principles. In this article, we consider ARMA processes in continuous time that are sampled at discrete-time intervals and provide conditions on the continuous-time process such that the results of Phillips and Solo can be utilized for normalized sums of the discrete-time observations. We utilize a state-space representation in the case of stock and flow variables, both of which are a linear combination of the state vector, and derive the relevant asymptotics based on multivariate extensions of the Phillips–Solo results. An illustrative application of the results to unit (zero) root testing is provided.

authors: Nicolas Inostroza; Anton Tsoy

abstract: Abstract An asset owner designs an asset-backed security and a signal about its value. After experiencing a liquidity shock and privately observing the signal, he sells the security to imperfectly competitive buyers. With flexible information design, the security’s informational sensitivity is a blessing, not a curse. Among double-monotone securities, the issuer prefers to sell the asset in combination with an appropriate signal rather than design more complex securities. Within the class of monotone securities, live-or-die securities are optimal and strictly dominate asset sales. When signals are restricted to be sufficiently informative about the upside, debt and additional-tier-1 debt become optimal. (JEL D82, D86, G32)

title: How Private Equity Fuels Nonbank Lending
authors: Sharjil Haque; Simon Mayer; Teng Wang
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System ,; Carnegie Mellon University Tepper School of Business, ,; University of Texas at Arlington ,
abstract: Abstract We demonstrate how private equity (PE) promotes nonbank lending by substituting for bank monitoring. Relative to non-PE-backed loans, PE-backed loans exhibit lower bank monitoring, smaller loan shares retained by lead banks, and larger shares held by nonbanks. The substitution is strongest when sponsors have greater incentives to engage with portfolio firms, is not associated with weaker loan performance, and persists during borrower distress. Our findings suggest that PE sponsors’ active engagement—through monitoring and support in distress—reduces banks’ need for monitoring and information production, enabling them to retain less skin in the game and sell loans to nonbanks.

title: Insurance and Assurance: Government Interventions and Depositor Behavior in Crisis
authors: Sümeyra Atmaca; Karolin Kirschenmann; Steven Ongena; Koen Schoors
affiliations: Ghent University , Tweekerkenstraat 2, 9000 Ghent, Belgium; University College Roosevelt , Lange Noordstraat 1, 4331 CB Middelburg, The Netherlands; ZEW Mannheim , L7,1, 68161 Mannheim, Germany; Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz , Jakob-Welder-Weg 4, 55128 Mainz, Germany; University of Zurich , Plattenstrasse 14, 8031 Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: Abstract We examine how different forms of government intervention - explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization - shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis. Using proprietary monthly account-level data, we show that depositors respond to formal insurance limits even in an environment of broad state support, but adjust only partially. Stabilization is markedly stronger after the takeover by a financially strong private bank than during state ownership, despite unchanged statutory coverage. These patterns are inconsistent with a strong bailout-expectations view in which explicit insurance is largely irrelevant and instead point to credibility as a key determinant of depositor behavior. We further show that political trust amplifies the effectiveness of government guarantees. Overall, our findings highlight that the form and credibility of government backstops, rather than coverage levels alone, are central to retail deposit funding stability during crises.

title: Does Free Speech Law Contribute to Corporate Social Responsibility Behavior? Empirical Evidence
authors: Paul A. Griffin; Hyun Hong; Boochun Jung; S. Katie Moon; Jiwoo Ryou
affiliations: University of California, Davis; University of California, Riverside; University of Hawaii at Manoa; Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology; West Virginia University
abstract: ABSTRACT People’s right to free speech can have profound effects on how firms discharge their social and environmental responsibilities. We examine these effects by analyzing the impact of the staggered enactment of anti-SLAPP free speech laws across U.S. states on firms’ corporate social responsibility (CSR) behavior. We theorize that, following the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, firms enhance their CSR activities as an economically effective means to counter negative publicity from stakeholders. Supporting this idea, we find that firm CSR activity increases after the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, accompanied by an increase in stakeholder criticism of firms’ social and environmental practices. Further, we observe an increase in the level of CSR disclosure. The link between anti-SLAPP law enactment and subsequent CSR engagement is stronger in states with more comprehensive anti-SLAPP protections than in those with weaker protections. title: Productivity versus Efficiency: The Effect of Incentive Focus on Target Setting in Participative Budgets
authors: Jake Andrassy; Jason L. Brown; Timothy Mallon; Ashley K. Sauciuc
affiliations: Texas State University; Indiana University Bloomington; Portland State University
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms typically design incentive systems to motivate employees and advance firm objectives, including productivity (i.e., maximizing output) and efficiency (i.e., minimizing input). However, there remains little empirical research on the potential psychological effects of adopting a productivity versus efficiency focus on employee risk perceptions and decision-making. To address this important gap, we examine how these different incentive foci affect employee target setting under participative budgets. We predict and find that employees perceive efficiency incentives as riskier than productivity incentives, leading to lower target setting. Moreover, consistent with our theory, this effect disappears in the absence of outcome uncertainty. We also find employees are less likely to achieve their target and have higher error rates under efficiency incentives, despite setting easier targets. Overall, our findings suggest that efficiency incentives, relative to productivity incentives, can have detrimental effects on target setting and subsequent performance in participative budgeting settings. title: How Black Accounting Faculty Exercise Agency to Navigate Career Advancement within Institutional Structures
authors: Michelle K. Harding; Jennifer R. Joe; Kerri-Ann Sanderson
affiliations: Virginia Tech; Bentley University
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how tenured BAF experience and navigate institutional structures while advancing their careers. Leveraging a qualitative approach, we find BAF encounter recurring forms of marginalization embedded in organizational structures that lead to social identity threats that destabilize their identities as scholars and teachers. BAF respond to these threats by employing agentic and self-preserving coping responses designed to affirm identity and negotiate career advancement. Although coping responses can be effective on an individual level, they do not transform institutional structures and can provoke pushback that reinscribes marginalization. The findings unsettle common assumptions that effort in conditions marked by objectivity and neutrality drives career advancement and highlight the institutional structures and invisible labor that BAF navigate to achieve career advancement. We fill the void in the literature examining how career advancement unfolds within racialized conditions of academic institutions and advance research on minoritized group status in accounting academia.

title: Internal Control over Financial Reporting and Mortgage Fraud
authors: Yiwei Dou; Danye Wang; Xi Wu
affiliations: New York University; The University of Iowa; University of California, Berkeley
abstract: ABSTRACT Mortgage fraud was a leading force behind the 2008 financial crisis. We measure the fraudulent income overstatement at the bank-ZIP Code-year level as the difference in the local growth between reported income in mortgage applications and the income based on IRS data. We find that overstated income is positively associated with banks’ internal control weaknesses over financial reporting and negatively associated with subsequent remediation of such weaknesses. The associations are concentrated among banks that integrate their accounting and operation processes, as proxied by the adoption of an Enterprise Resource Planning system. Finally, using the removal of internal control provisions in the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act in 2005 as a shock to internal control quality, we find that affected banks experience increased income overstatement on mortgage applications. Access to proprietary data is subject to the relevant providers’ licensing restrictions. JEL Classifications: G01; G21; G28; G51; M41.

title: On Liberalism’s Global Career: Dadabhai Naoroji and Representative Government
authors: TEJAS PARASHER
affiliations: University of California
abstract: This article reconsiders the relationship between the globalization of political liberalism and the globalization of political equality. Departing from interpretations of liberal theories of rights and representation as egalitarian or democratic, the article reconstructs an elitist paradigm of liberal representative government from the colonial world. It does so by offering a new reading of the thought of Indian political leader Dadabhai Naoroji. It recovers Naoroji’s overlooked commentary on political representation and imperial reform. I show that Naoroji drew upon analyses made by the first generation of Indian liberal thinkers about imperial political economy and mass-elite relations and used these arguments to formulate a distinctive model of electoral politics as a form of hierarchical tutelage. The recovery of Naoroji’s theory illustrates the deep tensions between representation and mass politics that marked liberalism’s global circulation.

title: The Ambiguities of Ownership and Class: A Reply to Nicholas Vrousalis
authors: CHIARA CORDELLI
affiliations: University of Chicago
abstract: The article replies to Nicholas Vrousalis’s attempt to rescue radical republicanism from my critique that it fails on three counts: its non-contingency, domination, and structural injustice theses. Central to my response are the claims that (i) capitalist power cannot be reduced to legal ownership of the means of production, as the process of capitalization is constitutive of capital; (ii) neither neo-republican nor Kantian notions of domination adequately capture what is inherently wrong with capitalism, and (iii) the concept of “class domination” remains theoretically puzzling. I then defend an alienation-centered critique: capitalism’s mode of investment subjects citizens to an impersonal and anarchical form of governance, which, by being necessarily alienating, contradicts democratic self-determination. Overall, this critique forms the core of a “political, political theory of capitalism” and grounds the case for a specific kind of democratic socialism—socialism as reconciliation—which is more demanding than both republican and liberal socialisms.

title: Framing Democracy: How Elites' Discourse Shapes Citizens' Understandings of Democracy and Enables Backsliding
authors: Selim Erdem Aytaç
abstract: abstract: Citizens' divergent understandings of democracy have important implications for democratic resilience, yet the sources of this heterogeneity remain contested. The author argues that partisan elite discourse is a key driver of these divergent understandings: political leaders' framing of democracy systematically shapes their supporters' democratic priorities. Observational and experimental evidence from Turkey supports this argument. The author establishes that Turkish party leaders differ in how they conceptualize democracy in public discourse, and these differences map onto their supporters' understandings of democracy. A population-based survey experiment shows that when leaders emphasize particular dimensions of democracy, copartisans also assign greater importance to those same dimensions of democratic governance. These findings highlight how partisan elite framing can influence mass conceptions of democracy in ways that enable democratic backsliding: would-be autocrats can exploit this dynamic to subvert liberal norms without significant backlash, even where overall support for democracy remains high.

title: The Paradox of Imperial Taxation: How Diversity Shaped Fiscal Development in the Ottoman Empire
authors: Yusuf Magiya
abstract: abstract: This article investigates the relationship between diversity and state building by examining how diversity affects the costs of investing in fiscal capacity. The author argues that diversity—ethnic or religious—makes populations less legible to the state, thereby increasing those costs. Higher costs deter the state from investing in fiscal capacity in more diverse areas, which hinders fiscal capacity building in those regions. Instead, the state diverts investments to less diverse areas, which are typically populated by the core/dominant group. As a result, the dominant group bears a higher tax burden compared to minority groups, which do not experience comparable tax increases. The author tests these arguments using original data on local-level fiscal revenues in the late Ottoman Empire along with qualitative and quantitative evidence from archival sources and contemporary cross-national and subnational data.

title: Political Socialization In Authoritarian Regimes: Sites and Everyday Experiences for Young People in Zimbabwe
authors: Marjoke Oosterom; Simbarashe Gukurume; Tinotenda Chishiri
abstract: abstract: Scholarship on political socialization has largely overlooked how forms of violence and repression experienced by young people living in authoritarian regimes affect their political development. Bringing together the literatures on political socialization and violence, this study aims to advance debates on youth political socialization in authoritarian regimes. How and where do young people in such contexts develop political orientations and behaviors, and through which mechanisms? To address these questions, this study draws on qualitative research with urban youths in Zimbabwe between 2019 and 2022 to demonstrate the significance of everyday encounters with authoritarianism in contested urban spaces. The authors advance existing scholarship by conceptualizing and analyzing diffuse socialization experiences and sites of socialization, showing how ruling party agents operating at urban markets use diverse socialization practices to cultivate loyalty to the ruling party among young traders. The authors argue that political socialization in this context does not foster genuine loyalty but provides tacit knowledge about authoritarian politics and how to navigate it through performative compliance.

title: Renewing Democracy: How Exposure to Electoral Turnovers Reinforces Citizens' Democratic Support
authors: Damien Bol
abstract: abstract: A prevailing narrative argues that citizens who live under democratic rule take it for granted, potentially leading to democratic backsliding. This article advances a more optimistic perspective, arguing that electoral turnovers—that is, elections that displace the head of government—reinforce democratic support. To test this argument, the author merges multiple international surveys that cover more than 350,000 respondents in seventy-nine countries, matches those surveys with a century's worth of electoral data, and identifies the national electoral turnovers to which each respondent was exposed throughout their life. Cohort analysis shows that exposure to turnovers, especially those that occur after prolonged periods of incumbency, has a positive and lasting effect on democratic support. Further analysis reveals that the effect is positive in a wide range of contexts, but is strongest among citizens who have always lived in a democracy. This finding thus suggests that frequent electoral turnovers are important to renew citizens' support for democracy.

title: When Does Civil Society Prevent Violence? Civic Networks, Demography, and Communal Conflict in Côte d'Ivoire
authors: Philip A. Martin
abstract: abstract: This article explores whether local civic networks can reduce the risk of violence in communally divided societies. The author argues that dense associational networks can foster intercommunal peace near elections, but only when those networks are situated in communities diverse enough that civic networks foster intergroup contact and monitoring by local elites. Leveraging new village-level data and interviews from Côte d'Ivoire, the author examines the relationship between the country's civic associations and the political violence that occurred during national elections in 2020 and 2021. Contrary to the arguments of civil society skeptics, he shows that robust networks of voluntary associations had significant spillover benefits for peace, particularly in communally diverse areas. However, in areas with a dominant communal group, civic networks had little impact on the risk of violence. The findings inform debates about the constraints on intercommunal conflict and the significance of associationalism in divided societies.
